newsitem.title: USA: NRC official leaked confidential information.
newsitem.headline: NRC official leaked confidential information.

text.p: A Nuclear Regulatory Commission official pleaded guilty Friday to providing confidential information to a Maine nuclear plant under investigation for safety problems.

Edouard Trottier gave Maine Yankee part of an NRC probe of testing of a key safety system because he wanted to "level the playing field" between the plant and the news media, according to U.S. Attorney Jay McCloskey.

McCloskey said Maine Yankee notified the NRC when it realised it was not supposed to have the information, but the report's disclosure may have "substantially" hurt an on-going Justice Department probe of the testing.

"They (Maine Yankee) were able to observe portions of this report, which included the indentities of certain people who had provided information," McCloskey told reporters. "Obviously you can't unring a bell."
Maine Yankee did not solicit the information and no other people were expected to be charged, although three copies were made of the report before the mistake was discovered, McCloskey said.
Trottier had been the NRC Project Manager for Maine Yankee for 13 years until he was suspended four months ago as part of the investigation. He pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court in Portland.

Trottier was the victim of a "misunderstanding," although he recognised he was "not going through channels" when he faxed the investigation report to Maine Yankee, Trottier's attorney, Peter DeTroy, told reporters.
"He thought that this report, and the information in it, was ultimately going to be released to the licensee and had been, or was about, to be released to the media," DeTroy said.
NRC officials declined to comment Friday, but said Trottier, 59, of Columbia, Md., was allowed to retire Feb. 28 with full benefits. Maine Yankee officials said they cooperated fully in the probe.

Maine Yankee came under intense public and regulatory scrutiny in late 1995 when an anonymous whistleblower wrote a letter that alleged engineers fraudently manipulated tests in the late 1980s on the emergency core cooling system.

Safety problems have forced the facility, in Wiscasset, Maine, to shut down several times in the past three years and the NRC recently placed it on the Watch List of troubled plants. It is currently off-line to fix misrouted electrical cables.

A special NRC reveiw conducted last year concluded that a "corporate culture" had develop at the 25-year-old plant that discouraged workers from reporting safety problems because of management pressure to cut costs.

Asked if Trottier's action showed NRC officials who oversee a plant for a long time could become too sympathetic to its management, McCloskey said, "I think you're stating the obvious and I'm sure that's occurred to the NRC."

Trottier will be sentenced later this year. He faces a maximum sentence of one year in prison and a $100,000 fine. The charge is a misdemeanor but McCloskey said he will press for jail time because he considers it "very serious."
McCloskey, whose office has been reviewing the whistle blower's allegations for several months, could not say when he expected the probe would be completed.
The 910-megawatt plant is owned by a coalition of New England utilities, including Central Maine Power, Bangor Hydro, Maine Public Service, Northeast Utilities and the New England Electric System.
